notes.claim: Design current is the magnitude of the current to be carried by a circuit in normal service; the course slides and an IET article give the same meaning.
For a three-phase load with known power factor and efficiency, Ib = P / (VL × Eff × PF × √3), where P is the output of the load and VL is the line-to-line voltage (400 V).
Motors need more current than expected for their output because of reactance, so power factor matters: a lower power factor means more apparent power, and so more current, for the same real power.

Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power, so the supply must provide more than the output; the slides show an efficiency and power factor left out would size the cable on 28.86 A rather than 41.47 A.
Three-phase real power is √3 × line voltage × line current × power factor, which is why Ib divides by √3 × VL × Eff × PF.
If a separate voltage is given, for example at a sub-board, that value is used in place of 230 V or 400 V; the slides work 20 kW at 393 V as 29.38 A.

In a balanced delta load the line current is the phase (winding) current times the square root of 3, so each winding carries the line current divided by √3; in star the line and phase currents are equal.
Diversity percentages are only found in the On-Site Guide and are guidance that need not be applied; the slides' example designs ten 100 W lamps at 66%, or 660 W, rather than 1000 W.
For i1 (review fix): the slides' 66% diversity example is for a domestic lighting circuit, from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A.

For i1 (review fix): at a reduced voltage a resistive heater draws proportionally less current, while a motor draws more to keep its torque, so the slides' same-power working at a sub-board's voltage errs on the safe side for a heater.

For i1 (review fix): the showroom's motor is controlled by a star-delta starter, which runs six wires to the motor, one to each end of each winding, so in delta each of those cables carries one winding's current.
